title: How to Track WPForms in GTM With Clean Enhanced Conversions Data
intro:
WPForms has an odd way of naming things. Look at a lead's data in the browser and the email field isn't called email. It's wpforms[fields][1]. The next field is wpforms[fields][2], and the numbers change from form to form.

That was the problem on a client's WordPress site where every lead came through WPForms. To send Enhanced Conversions data, I needed to know which field was which, on any form, without keeping a map. So the listener reads the label the visitor sees instead.

This walkthrough shows that setup, using the client's real container with the names removed.
tldr: Add one free Custom HTML tag and trigger on wpforms_form_success. It handles AJAX forms, page reloads and thank-you redirects, and reads fields by their visible labels. Send form details to GA4 and the normalized contact fields to Enhanced Conversions, then check the values in Preview.
sections: Why a click or thank-you trigger isn't enough

WPForms can finish a submission in different ways, and a single GTM trigger type won't cover them all. Here's what the listener looks for:

What the form doesSignalec_detection_method
AJAX submitjQuery wpformsAjaxSubmitSuccessconfirmation_event
Confirmation renders.wpforms-confirmation-containerconfirmation_class
Page reload or thank-you pageMatched to data saved at submitstored_recall
Form disappears or page leaves after submitInferred. Turn off with strictSuccess: trueform_removed, pagehide

Failed submissions get their own event, wpforms_form_failed, which lists the fields that failed.

Other options exist. This guide pushes an event from each form's confirmation message, sending only a form name. The AVAK plugin tracks submissions and errors as metadata, and says it doesn't collect personal data. Both are fine for counting. I needed contact data from one GTM tag, with no change to each form.

1. Download the GTM tag, or get it from GitHub.
  2. Create a Custom HTML tag and paste it. The wrapper and config are included.
  3. Fire it on All Pages, so it can also finish the job on a thank-you page.
[[img:wpf-listener-tag|The tag on the client's container, which runs an earlier v3 build. The download is v3.3.0.]]

The defaults are safe to leave. Set debug: true only while testing. If the site runs another form tool too, use the universal listener instead, and never both.

Go to Triggers > New > Custom Event and use wpforms_form_success. On this site, every lead tag hangs off that one trigger.

[[img:wpf-trigger|One trigger, used by GA4, Google Ads and an OpenAI Ads pixel.]]
Step 3: Send it to GA4 and Google Ads

Create a GA4 Event tag on the trigger, with form_id, form_cta and form_platform as parameters. Keep the ec_* contact fields out of it, because GA4's terms prohibit personal data.

Then add a Google Ads Conversion Tracking tag on the same trigger, with a Conversion Linker on all pages.

[[img:wpf-gads-tag|The website lead conversion. Label hidden.]]

Want these in reports? GA4 won't show them until you register each one as a custom dimension. Here's how.

This is where the label matching pays off. A field labelled Email Address, or a Name field with First and Last sub-labels, becomes a clean key, whatever number WPForms gave it:

dataLayer keyHolds
ec_emailEmail, lowercased and checked
ec_phonePhone in E.164
ec_first_name, ec_last_nameName, split where possible
ec_street, ec_city, ec_region, ec_postal_code, ec_countryAddress, if the form has it

Create a Data Layer Variable for each one you use, then a User-Provided Data variable set to Manual configuration. Use it in a Google Ads User-provided Data Event tag on the same trigger, as this site does, or on the conversion tag.

[[img:wpf-ec-tag|The enhanced conversion tag, firing on the same event.]]

Clear labels help. A field labelled just Contact is harder to classify than one labelled Phone Number, so check the values in the next step. If you see ec_pii_redacted, or a field holding the wrong value, the Gravity Forms walkthrough shows the two causes I've found and how to spot them.

1. In Preview, load a form page and expect ec_tracker_initialized.
  2. Submit with a required field empty. Expect wpforms_form_failed.
  3. Submit a labelled test lead. Expect one wpforms_form_success.
  4. Open that event and read ec_email, ec_phone and the name fields.
  5. Refresh the confirmation page. Expect nothing new.

To see consent state, attached forms and the last event, run:

window._ecFormTrackers.wpforms.status()

Then remove any older click or thank-you conversions for the same form, and publish. Here's the finished setup:

[[img:wpf-tag-list|One listener with GA4, Google Ads and other platforms working from its event. IDs anonymised.]]

• The client's container runs an earlier v3 build, and I didn't place a new test lead for this post. Test v3.3.0 on your own forms.
  • Without jQuery on the page, AJAX success relies on the confirmation container appearing.
  • A redirect to another domain can't use the saved data.
  • Bot or spam submissions that pass WPForms' validation still count.

It's free, MIT licensed and on GitHub.

Can GTM's built-in Form Submission trigger track WPForms?

It can fire, but not reliably on every confirmation type. AJAX forms often don't produce a standard submit, and a submit event doesn't prove the entry was accepted. The listener waits for WPForms' own confirmation.

Does this send WPForms leads to Google Ads?

Yes. Put your Google Ads conversion tag on wpforms_form_success, and map the ec_* keys for Enhanced Conversions.
